cdsa.2: Defines the terms used in the Act, including 'controlled substance' (Schedules I to IV and Part 1 of Schedule V), 'precursor' (Part 2 of Schedule V or Schedule VI), 'designated substance offence' (any Part I offence except simple possession under s. 4(1), plus conspiracy, attempt, accessory after the fact and counselling), 'offence-related property' (property other than a controlled substance used in, by means of, or intended for a designated substance offence, split into chemical and non-chemical), 'possession' (as in s. 4(3) of the Criminal Code), 'practitioner', 'analyst', 'inspector' and 'adjudicator'.
cdsa.3: Any power or duty that can be exercised for an offence under the Act can also be exercised for a conspiracy or attempt to commit it, being an accessory after the fact, or counselling it.
cdsa.4: Bans possessing a Schedule I, II or III substance unless authorized under the regulations, and bans getting a Schedule I-IV substance or a prescription for one from a practitioner without disclosing other substances or prescriptions obtained in the previous 30 days. Possession of a Schedule I substance carries up to 7 years on indictment, Schedule II up to 5 years less a day, Schedule III up to 3 years. On summary conviction the limit is a fine of up to $1,000 or 6 months for a first offence and up to $2,000 or 1 year for a subsequent one. Obtaining without disclosure carries up to 7 years (Schedule I), 5 years less a day (II), 3 years (III) or 18 months (IV) on indictment, with the same summary penalties.
cdsa.5: Bans trafficking in a Schedule I-V substance, or in anything represented as one, and bans possessing such a substance for the purpose of trafficking. For Schedule I or II substances the maximum is life imprisonment. For Schedule III or V it is up to 10 years on indictment or up to 18 months on summary conviction. For Schedule IV it is up to 3 years on indictment or up to 1 year on summary conviction.
cdsa.6: Bans importing or exporting a Schedule I-VI substance, and possessing one for the purpose of exporting it, unless authorized under the regulations. For Schedule I or II substances the maximum is life imprisonment. For Schedule III, V or VI it is up to 10 years on indictment or up to 18 months on summary conviction. For Schedule IV it is up to 3 years on indictment or up to 1 year on summary conviction.
cdsa.7: Bans producing a Schedule I-V substance unless authorized under the regulations. For Schedule I or II substances the maximum is life imprisonment. For Schedule III or V it is up to 10 years on indictment or up to 18 months on summary conviction. For Schedule IV it is up to 3 years on indictment or up to 1 year on summary conviction.
cdsa.9: Requires a parliamentary committee to undertake a comprehensive review of the Act within five years of the section coming into force, including a cost-benefit analysis of mandatory minimum sentences, and to report to Parliament within a year of starting the review.
cdsa.10: Sets the purpose of sentencing for offences under Part I: respect for the law and a just, peaceful and safe society, while encouraging rehabilitation and treatment where appropriate and acknowledging harm to victims and the community. On a designated substance offence the court must consider aggravating factors, including carrying or using a weapon, using or threatening violence, trafficking (or possessing for trafficking) in or near a school or other place young people usually gather or to a person under 18, a prior designated substance offence, and using or involving someone under 18. If it finds such a factor but does not imprison, the court must give reasons. The court may also delay sentencing so the offender can take part in an approved drug treatment court program or a treatment program.
cdsa.11: A justice may issue a search warrant, on an ex parte application supported by information on oath, where there are reasonable grounds to believe a controlled substance or precursor, something containing it, offence-related property, or evidence of an offence under the Act (or of Criminal Code ss. 354 and 462.31 tied to it) is in a place. Applications by telecommunication follow s. 487.1 of the Criminal Code, and the warrant can be executed anywhere in Canada by an officer with authority there. An officer may search a person found there who is believed to have the items on them, and may seize items not named in the warrant that they reasonably believe are contraband, containers of it, offence-related property or evidence. Where exigent circumstances make a warrant impracticable, the officer may use these powers without one.
cdsa.12: When exercising the search powers in s. 11, a peace officer may enlist the assistance they consider necessary and use as much force as is necessary in the circumstances.
cdsa.13: Sections 489.1 and 490 of the Criminal Code (reporting and detention of seized things) apply to things seized under this Act, subject to ss. 16 to 22 and 31(6) to (9) for non-chemical offence-related property. Where a controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property is seized under any authority, the Act's own rules and regulations apply to it. A judge or justice ordering return of property under s. 490(9)(c) may require the applicant to enter a recognizance.
cdsa.14: The Attorney General may apply, ex parte and in writing to a judge with an affidavit, for a restraint order prohibiting dealing with non-chemical offence-related property. The judge may make the order on reasonable grounds to believe the property is offence-related, including for property outside Canada, and may attach conditions. The order must be in writing, served as the judge directs, and registered against the property under provincial law. It stays in effect until an order is made under s. 19(3), 19.1(3) or s. 490(9) or (11) of the Criminal Code, or forfeiture is ordered. Knowingly breaching a served restraint order is a hybrid offence.
cdsa.15: Sections 489.1 and 490 of the Criminal Code apply, with necessary modifications and subject to ss. 16 to 22, to property under a s. 14 restraint order. On an order to return such property, the judge or justice may require the applicant to enter a recognizance or deposit security.
cdsa.16: If a person is convicted of (or discharged under s. 730 of the Criminal Code for) a designated substance offence, and the court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities that non-chemical offence-related property is related to the offence, it must order forfeiture on the Attorney General's application, to the province or to Canada depending on who prosecuted. Where the link to the offence is not established on that standard, the court may still order forfeiture if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the property is non-chemical offence-related property. Orders may cover property outside Canada. The convicted person or the Attorney General may appeal the order, or a failure to make one, to the court of appeal as if it were a sentence appeal.
cdsa.17: If an information has been laid for a designated substance offence, the Attorney General may apply for forfeiture without a conviction. The judge must order forfeiture if satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the property is non-chemical offence-related property, that proceedings were started for the related offence, and that the accused has died or absconded. An accused is deemed to have absconded once an arrest warrant has been outstanding for six months despite reasonable attempts to arrest. Forfeited property goes to the province or to Canada depending on who commenced the proceedings, and the order can cover property outside Canada.
cdsa.18: Before ordering forfeiture under s. 16(1) or 17(2), a court may set aside any transfer of the property made after it was seized or restrained, unless it was for valuable consideration to a person acting in good faith.
cdsa.19: Before ordering forfeiture under s. 16(1) or 17(2), the court must require notice to anyone who appears to have a valid interest in the property. It may return the property, or part of it, to a lawful owner or lawful possessor who appears innocent of any complicity or collusion and is not the accused or someone who took the property from the accused to avoid forfeiture.
cdsa.20: A person claiming an interest in forfeited property (other than the convicted or charged person, or someone who got the property from them to avoid forfeiture) may apply to a judge within 30 days of the forfeiture. The hearing is set at least 30 days after filing and the Attorney General must get at least 15 days' notice. If the applicant appears innocent of any complicity in the offence and exercised all reasonable care to be satisfied the property was not likely to be used unlawfully, the judge may declare that their interest is not affected by the forfeiture and declare its nature, extent or value. The applicant or the Attorney General may appeal, and once appeal periods have ended the Minister must direct that the property be returned or that the value of the interest be paid.
cdsa.21: A person aggrieved by an in rem forfeiture order under s. 17(2) may appeal as if it were an appeal against conviction or against a judgment or verdict of acquittal under Part XXI of the Criminal Code, which applies with necessary modifications.
cdsa.22: An order in respect of property under s. 16(1), 17(2) or 20(4) is suspended while any application about the property or any appeal from a forfeiture or restoration order is pending, and the property cannot be disposed of until 30 days after an order is made.
cdsa.23: A peace officer, inspector or prescribed person may return a seized or found controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property to its lawful owner or lawful possessor if there is no dispute about who that is and it is not needed for proceedings. They must get a receipt, and for a seizure under s. 11, the Criminal Code or common law, must report the return to a justice.
cdsa.24: Within 60 days of a seizure, finding or acquisition, anyone may apply in writing to a justice (after notifying the Attorney General) for return of a controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property. If the applicant is the lawful owner or lawful possessor and the Attorney General does not say it may be needed for proceedings, the justice orders it returned as soon as practicable. If it may be needed, the order is for return after 180 days if no proceeding has started, or at the conclusion of any proceeding in which the applicant is not found guilty of an offence related to it. If the applicant is not the lawful owner or possessor, and it is not needed, the justice orders it forfeited to the Crown. If it was already disposed of under s. 26, the justice orders payment of its value to an applicant who is the lawful owner or possessor.
cdsa.25: If no application for return is made within 60 days of the seizure, finding or acquisition, and the substance, precursor or property is not needed for proceedings, it is forfeited to the Crown and disposed of under the regulations or as the Minister directs.
cdsa.26: A precursor or chemical offence-related property whose storage or handling poses a risk to health or safety, or a controlled substance, that is not needed for proceedings may be disposed of by the Minister, a peace officer or a prescribed person under the regulations or as the Minister directs.
cdsa.27: When a court finds that a controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property is no longer needed in proceedings, it must order it returned to the person it was seized from if they obtained and dealt with it lawfully, or to the lawful owner if the holder's possession was unlawful and the owner is known. Otherwise the court may order it forfeited to the Crown.
cdsa.28: If a seized or found controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property is not needed for proceedings, its lawful owner may consent to its disposition, and it is then forfeited to the Crown and disposed of under the regulations or as the Minister directs.
cdsa.29: Within 30 days of disposing of or otherwise dealing with a controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property under this Division, the peace officer, inspector or prescribed person must send the Minister a report covering what it was, how much, how it was dealt with, when, which agency and the file number. Using it to conduct an investigation or for training counts as dealing with it.
cdsa.30: The Minister may designate any person as an inspector under the regulations. Every inspector gets a certificate of designation and must produce it on request when entering a place under s. 31(1).
cdsa.31: An inspector may enter a place, including a conveyance, to verify compliance or prevent non-compliance with the Act or regulations, and may open and examine receptacles and packages, examine things used or capable of being used to produce, preserve, package or store controlled substances or precursors, examine and copy labels, advertising, records and electronic data (other than medical records of persons), photograph and record, take samples for analysis, seize and detain substances, precursors, designated devices or conveyances, order things or conveyances to be moved or not moved, order people to establish their identity, and order a person to stop or start an activity covered by the Act. Entry is limited to places where the inspector reasonably believes a controlled substance, precursor, designated device or administration-related document is located, or an activity could be conducted under a licence, permit, authorization or exemption the Minister is considering, among the other cases listed.
cdsa.32: No person may obstruct an inspector carrying out their powers or duties, knowingly make a false or misleading statement to an inspector, or without the inspector's authority remove, alter or interfere with anything seized, detained or taken under s. 31.
cdsa.33: The Governor in Council may designate a regulation made under the Act as a 'designated regulation', the contravention of which is dealt with under this Part.
cdsa.34: If the Minister has reasonable grounds to believe a person contravened a designated regulation, the Minister must serve a notice to appear on the person and send a copy to an adjudicator, directing the adjudicator to hold a hearing on whether the contravention occurred.
cdsa.35: If the Minister has reasonable grounds to believe a designated regulation was contravened and that it creates a substantial risk of immediate danger to health or safety, the Minister may, without prior notice, make an interim order prohibiting the person from doing what their licence, permit or authorization would allow, or imposing conditions on it, including suspending, cancelling or amending that licence, permit or authorization. The Minister must promptly serve the order and a notice to appear and send both to an adjudicator for a hearing.
cdsa.36: An adjudicator who receives a notice to appear holds a hearing on a date fixed at the person's request. For a s. 34 notice, the hearing is between 30 and 45 days after service, and for an interim order notice it is between 3 and 45 days after service. If the person does not request a date within 45 days, or fails to appear, the adjudicator decides in their absence. The adjudicator sets the time and place, subject to the regulations.
cdsa.37: A notice to appear served on a person under s. 34(a) or 35(2)(b) must name the designated regulation the Minister believes was contravened, state the grounds, state that the matter has been referred to an adjudicator for a hearing within the applicable period in s. 36(1), and include any other prescribed information.
cdsa.38: Proof of service of any notice, order or interim order under this Part must be given in the prescribed manner.
cdsa.39: For the purposes of the Act, an adjudicator has the powers of a commissioner appointed under Part I of the Inquiries Act.
cdsa.40: An adjudicator must deal with all matters as informally and expeditiously as the circumstances and considerations of fairness and natural justice permit.
cdsa.41: After a hearing (or a proceeding held in the person's absence), the adjudicator must decide within the prescribed time whether the person contravened the designated regulation, and promptly notify the person and the Minister with reasons. If the adjudicator finds a contravention, the person is told they may make written representations to the Minister. The Minister must then consider the determination and representations and make an order prohibiting the person from doing what they would otherwise be permitted to do, or imposing terms and conditions, which may include suspending, cancelling or amending a licence, permit or authorization. The order is served on the person in the prescribed manner.
cdsa.42: An interim order under s. 35(1) and a Minister's order under s. 41(3) take effect when served. An interim order ceases to have effect when the Minister's s. 41(3) order is served, or when the adjudicator determines there was no contravention. A person subject to a s. 41(3) order may apply in writing to the Minister to revoke it, and the Minister may revoke it in whole or in part in the prescribed circumstances.
cdsa.43: It is an offence to contravene an order or interim order made under this Part.
cdsa.44: The Minister may designate any person as an analyst for the purposes of the Act and regulations, in accordance with the regulations.
cdsa.45: A peace officer, inspector or prescribed person may submit a substance, or a sample of it, to an analyst for analysis or examination. The analyst may prepare a certificate or report stating that the analysis was done and giving the results.
cdsa.46: Sets the general penalty for contravening a provision of the Act with no other punishment, a provision of a regulation, or an order under s. 45.1 or 45.2. On indictment: a fine of up to $5,000,000, or imprisonment for up to 3 years, or both. On summary conviction: for a first offence, a fine of up to $250,000 or up to 6 months, or both; for a subsequent offence, a fine of up to $500,000 or up to 18 months, or both.
cdsa.47: Summary conviction proceedings for an offence under s. 4(2) or 32(2) or the regulations, or for contravening an order under s. 45.1 or 45.2, must start within one year after the subject matter arose. Proceedings for a contravention of the Act, regulations or such an order may be held where the offence was committed or the subject matter arose, or wherever the accused is apprehended or happens to be.
cdsa.48: An exception, exemption, excuse or qualification prescribed by law does not have to be set out or negatived in an information or indictment for an offence under the Act or regulations (or ss. 463 to 465 of the Criminal Code in respect of one). The prosecutor also does not have to prove, except in rebuttal, that a certificate, licence, permit or other qualification does not operate in the accused's favour.
cdsa.49: A copy of a document filed with a provincial or municipal body, or a statement from its records, purporting to be certified by the official with custody, is admissible in a prosecution for an offence referred to in s. 48(1) and is proof of the facts in it absent evidence to the contrary, without proof of the signature or official character. A reproduced facsimile signature is enough for authentication. The section does not make admissible a record made in the course of an investigation or inquiry.
cdsa.50: A certificate or other document issued under regulations made under s. 55(2)(c) or (2.1)(c) is admissible in any proceeding under this or another federal Act and, absent contrary evidence, proves it was validly issued and the facts in it, without proof of signature or official character. With leave of the court, the defence may require the issuer to produce an affidavit or solemn declaration, or to appear for examination or cross-examination.
cdsa.51: An analyst's certificate or report under s. 45(2) is admissible in any prosecution under this or another federal Act and, absent contrary evidence, proves the statements in it without proof of signature or official character. The party it is produced against may, with leave of the court, require the analyst to attend for cross-examination.
cdsa.52: Giving notice, orally or in writing, or serving a document can be proved by the oral evidence, affidavit or solemn declaration of the person who gave it or served it. The court may still require that person to appear for examination or cross-examination.
cdsa.53: Continuity of possession of an exhibit can be proved by the testimony, affidavit or solemn declaration of the person who had it. The court may require an affiant or declarant to appear for examination or cross-examination on continuity.
cdsa.54: When a record, book, electronic data or other document is examined or seized under the Act or regulations, the Minister or the officer may make copies. A copy purporting to be certified by the Minister or a person the Minister authorizes is admissible and, absent contrary evidence, has the same probative force as the original.
cdsa.55: Gives the Governor in Council broad power to make regulations to carry out the Act, including regulating the medical, scientific and industrial uses and distribution of controlled substances and precursors, enforcement, and designated devices. This covers controlling the importation, exportation, production, packaging, transportation, sale, provision, possession and other dealing in controlled substances and precursors, and the issuing, suspending, cancelling and terms of licences and authorizations for dealing in Schedule I to VI substances.
cdsa.56: The Minister may exempt any person, class of persons, controlled substance or precursor from all or some provisions of the Act or regulations, on terms the Minister considers necessary, if the exemption is necessary for a medical or scientific purpose or is otherwise in the public interest. A medical-purpose exemption cannot allow activities at a supervised consumption site involving a substance obtained in a manner not authorized under the Act.
cdsa.57: The Minister's powers, duties or functions under the Act or regulations, and those of the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness under the regulations, may be exercised by any person, or person holding a position, designated for that purpose by the relevant Minister.
cdsa.58: If this Act or its regulations conflict with the Food and Drugs Act or its regulations, this Act and its regulations prevail to the extent of the conflict.
cdsa.60: The Governor in Council may by order add items to or delete items from Schedules I to IV, VI and IX if it considers the amendment necessary in the public interest.
cdsa.61: References in a Criminal Code Part VI designation to an offence under the Narcotic Control Act or Part III or IV of the Food and Drugs Act, or to a conspiracy, attempt, accessory after the fact or counselling of one, are deemed to be references to an offence under s. 5 (trafficking), s. 6 (importing and exporting) or s. 7 (production) of this Act, as the case may be, or a conspiracy, attempt, accessory after the fact or counselling of one.
cdsa.62: If someone committed an offence under the Narcotic Control Act or Part III or IV of the Food and Drugs Act before this Act came into force and had not yet been sentenced, the sentence is imposed under this Act. But where this Act varies a penalty, forfeiture or punishment from the old law, the lesser one applies to offences committed before sections 4 to 9 came into force.
cdsa.63: Authorizations issued by the Minister under the listed provisions of the Food and Drug Regulations and Narcotic Control Regulations before sections 81 and 94 of this Act came into force are declared validly issued, and those still in force continue as if they were exemptions under s. 56.
cdsa.4.1: Protects a person who calls for emergency medical or law enforcement help for a life-threatening reaction to a psychoactive substance, and anyone else at the scene when help arrives, from being charged or convicted of simple possession under s. 4(1) where the evidence came from the call or from staying at the scene. It also bars charges for breaching pre-trial release or probation conditions related to a s. 4(1) offence in the same circumstances, and deems those conditions (including conditional sentence and parole conditions) not to be violated.
cdsa.7.1: Bans possessing, producing, selling, importing or transporting anything intending it to be used to produce a controlled substance (unless the production is lawfully authorized) or to traffic in one. For Schedule I, II, III or V substances the maximum is 10 years on indictment or 18 months on summary conviction. For Schedule IV it is 3 years on indictment or 1 year on summary conviction.
cdsa.10.1: Sets out principles for Part I: problematic substance use is primarily a health and social issue; interventions should be evidence-based and protect health, dignity and human rights; criminal sanctions for personal-use possession can increase stigma and are not consistent with public health evidence; interventions should address root causes; and judicial resources are better used on offences that risk public safety.
cdsa.10.2: Before laying an information for simple possession under s. 4(1), a peace officer must consider, in light of the s. 10.1 principles, taking no further action, giving a warning, or (with consent) referring the person to a community program or service. Failing to consider these options does not invalidate later charges.
cdsa.10.3: A prosecution for simple possession under s. 4(1) can start or continue only if the prosecutor, having regard to the s. 10.1 principles, considers that a warning, referral or alternative measures is not appropriate and that prosecution is.
cdsa.10.4: The police force must keep a record of each warning or referral under s. 10.2. The record can be made available to a court, a peace officer administering the case, and government bodies running alternative measures or preparing a report for the proceedings. Non-identifying information may be shared for assessing and researching alternative measures.
cdsa.10.5: Evidence of a warning or referral, of a decision to take no further action on a s. 4(1) possession offence, and of the offence itself cannot be used in court to prove prior offending behaviour.
cdsa.10.6: Records of s. 4(1) possession convictions are to be kept separate from other conviction records. For convictions before the section came into force this applies within two years of that day. For later convictions, it applies two years after the conviction or after the sentence expires, whichever is later, and the person is deemed never to have been convicted. The Governor in Council may make regulations on using, removing or destroying those records.
cdsa.10.7: A social worker, medical professional or other community service provider does not commit a s. 4(1) possession offence if, in the course of their duties, they come into possession of a Schedule I, II or III substance and intend to lawfully dispose of it within a reasonable period.
cdsa.12.1: Within 30 days, a peace officer, inspector or prescribed person who seizes, finds or acquires a controlled substance, precursor or chemical offence-related property must prepare a report (what, how much, where, when, which agency, file number) and send it to the Minister. If the seizure was under s. 11, the Criminal Code or common law, a copy goes to a justice as well.
cdsa.15.1: On application of the Attorney General, a justice (for property seized under s. 11 or at common law) or a judge (for property restrained under s. 14) may appoint a person to take control of and manage non-chemical offence-related property and require those holding it to hand it over. The manager may make an interlocutory sale of perishable or rapidly depreciating property, apply for a destruction order for property of little or no value (the court must order destruction if satisfied it has little or no value, after notice), and apply for forfeiture of property other than real property or a conveyance if notice gave a 60-day period to assert an interest and no one did. The order ends when the property is returned, destroyed or forfeited, and applies to net proceeds of any sale.
cdsa.19.1: Where property that would be forfeited is a dwelling-house, the court must require notice to members of the accused's immediate family who live there and may hear them. If forfeiting real property would be disproportionate to the nature and gravity of the offence, the circumstances and the accused's record, the court may decline to order forfeiture of the property or part of it, and may revoke the restraint order. For a dwelling-house the court must also consider the impact on immediate family members for whom it was the principal residence, and whether they appear innocent of any complicity or collusion.
cdsa.45.1: The Minister may order a person authorized under the Act to conduct activities with controlled substances or precursors, or a person who imports designated devices, to provide information about those activities within the time and in the manner the Minister sets, where needed to verify or prevent non-compliance or to address a public health or safety issue.
cdsa.45.2: The Minister may order a person authorized under the Act to conduct activities with controlled substances or precursors to take specified measures, within the time and in the manner the Minister sets, to prevent non-compliance or, on reasonable grounds to believe there is non-compliance, to remedy it.
cdsa.45.3: The Minister may designate any qualified individual or class of qualified individuals as review officers to review orders under s. 45.4.
cdsa.45.4: An order under s. 45.1 or 45.2 is reviewed by a review officer other than the person who made it, on the written request of the person ordered, but only on grounds of fact or mixed fact and law. The request must state the grounds and supporting evidence and reach the Minister within seven days of the order being provided. A review is not done if the request does not comply, or is frivolous, vexatious or not in good faith, and the person must be told why in writing. A review officer may also review an order on their own initiative. The order stays in effect during the review unless the review officer decides otherwise. The review must be completed within 30 days of the request reaching the Minister, extendable by up to 30 days at a time with written reasons. The officer may confirm, amend, terminate or cancel the order, and an amended order can be reviewed again.
cdsa.45.5: The Statutory Instruments Act does not apply to an order made under s. 45.1 or 45.2.
cdsa.46.1: No person may knowingly make, or take part in, agree to or acquiesce in the making of, a false or misleading statement in any book, record, return or other document that must be kept, made or provided under the Act or the regulations.
cdsa.46.2: The holder of a licence, permit, authorization or exemption must comply with its terms and conditions.
cdsa.46.3: No person may import a designated device into Canada without registering the importation with the Minister. The registration must include the importer's name and address, a description of the device (model, serial number, brand), the delivery and use addresses, the customs office and the anticipated date of importation. The Minister registers the importation and provides proof of registration, which the importer must give to the customs office. The Minister may refuse or cancel registration if false or misleading information was provided or to protect public health or safety, and may share the information with the Canada Border Services Agency and, on request in an investigation, with a police force.
cdsa.54.1: The Minister may engage people with technical or specialized knowledge to advise on the Minister's powers, duties or functions under the Act, and, with Treasury Board approval, fix their remuneration.
cdsa.56.1: For a supervised consumption site, the Minister may grant an exemption on terms the Minister considers necessary, where needed for a medical purpose, covering persons or classes of persons in relation to a controlled substance or precursor obtained in a manner not authorized under the Act, or the substance itself. An application must include the intended public health benefits and, if any, information on the site's impact on crime rates, local need, administrative structure, resources and community support or opposition. An application to continue activities must include updates since the previous exemption.
cdsa.60.1: The Minister may by order add an item to Schedule V for up to one year, extendable by up to another year, if there are reasonable grounds to believe it poses a significant risk to public health or safety, or may pose a risk and is being imported or distributed in Canada with no legitimate purpose. The Minister may also delete items. An item leaves Schedule V on the earliest of the day specified in a deletion order, the day it is added to another Schedule, and the end of its period.
cdsa.60.2: The Governor in Council may make regulations authorizing the Minister to add to or delete from, by order, any schedule to a regulation made under the Act any substance in Schedule V, and to make related consequential amendments to those schedules.

ycja.2: Defines the terms used in the Act. A 'young person' is a person who is, or appears to be, 12 years old or older but under 18, and includes anyone charged or found guilty under the Act for an offence committed while a young person. A 'child' is under 12. An 'adult sentence' is any sentence that could be imposed on an adult convicted of the same offence. The 'Attorney General' is defined as in s. 2 of the Criminal Code, extended to cover extrajudicial measures. A 'conference' is a group convened to give advice under s. 19, and 'extrajudicial measures' are measures other than judicial proceedings (including extrajudicial sanctions). A 'parent' includes anyone with a legal duty to provide for the young person or with legal or actual custody or control. The 'custodial portion' of a youth sentence under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) is the part served in custody before supervision in the community.
ycja.3: Sets out the principles of the youth criminal justice system. It exists to protect the public by holding young persons accountable through measures proportionate to the seriousness of the offence and their degree of responsibility, promoting rehabilitation and reintegration, and referring them to community programs that address the circumstances underlying their offending. It must be separate from the adult system, based on diminished moral blameworthiness, and emphasize rehabilitation and reintegration, fair and proportionate accountability, enhanced procedural protection (including privacy), timely intervention, and promptness. Measures should reinforce respect for societal values, encourage repair of harm, be meaningful for the individual young person, and respect their needs and characteristics, with particular attention to Aboriginal and Black young persons. Young persons have rights in their own right, including to be heard, and victims should be treated with courtesy, compassion, fairness and respect.
ycja.4: Declares principles for this Part (extrajudicial measures): they are often the most appropriate and effective response to youth crime, allow timely intervention focused on correcting behaviour, are presumed adequate to hold a young person accountable for a non-violent offence if they have no prior finding of guilt, and should be used where adequate, even if the young person has been dealt with by extrajudicial measures or found guilty before.
ycja.5: Extrajudicial measures should provide an effective and timely response outside the judicial system, encourage young persons to acknowledge and repair harm, involve families and the community, give victims a chance to take part in decisions and receive reparation, and respect the young person's rights and be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence.
ycja.6: Before starting judicial proceedings or taking other measures against a young person, a police officer must consider whether it is enough to take no further action, warn the young person, give a caution (if a program exists under s. 7) or, with the young person's consent, refer them to a community program or agency, having regard to ss. 4 and 4.1. Failing to consider these options does not invalidate later charges.
ycja.7: The Attorney General, or another minister designated by the lieutenant governor of a province, may set up a program allowing police to administer cautions to young persons instead of starting judicial proceedings.
ycja.8: The Attorney General may set up a program allowing prosecutors to administer cautions to young persons instead of starting or continuing judicial proceedings.
ycja.9: Evidence that a young person received a warning, caution or referral under ss. 6 to 8, that police took no further action, or of the offence itself, cannot be used in court to prove prior offending behaviour.
ycja.10: An extrajudicial sanction may be used only when a warning, caution or referral is not adequate because of the seriousness of the offence, the nature and number of previous offences or other aggravating circumstances. It must be part of an authorized program, be appropriate for the young person's needs and society's interests, and be freely consented to by a young person who was told of the right to counsel, had a chance to consult counsel and accepts responsibility for the act or omission. The Attorney General must also be of the opinion that there is sufficient evidence to prosecute and that prosecution is not barred at law. It cannot be used if the young person denies involvement or wants the charge dealt with by a youth justice court. Admissions made as a condition of extrajudicial measures are inadmissible in civil or criminal proceedings. A sanction does not bar judicial proceedings, but if charged, the court must dismiss the charge if the young person totally complied, and may dismiss it if they partially complied and prosecution would be unfair.
ycja.11: If a young person is dealt with by an extrajudicial sanction, the person running the program must tell a parent of the young person.
ycja.12: If a young person is dealt with by an extrajudicial sanction, a police officer, the Attorney General, the provincial director or a provincial victim-assistance organization must tell the victim, if the victim wishes, who the young person is and how the offence was dealt with.
ycja.13: A youth justice court is any court established or designated by or under provincial law, or designated by the Governor in Council or a provincial lieutenant governor in council, for the purposes of the Act. When a young person elects trial by judge alone, the judge (a s. 552 Criminal Code judge, or a superior court judge for s. 469 offences) is deemed a youth justice court judge; when the young person elects or is deemed to elect trial by judge and jury, the superior court of criminal jurisdiction is deemed the youth justice court.
ycja.14: A youth justice court has exclusive jurisdiction over any offence alleged to have been committed while the person was a young person, despite other Acts but subject to the Contraventions Act and the National Defence Act. It also has exclusive jurisdiction to make recognizance orders against a young person under ss. 83.3 and 810 to 810.2 of the Criminal Code. If the young person refuses to enter into the recognizance, the court may impose a s. 42(2) sanction, with a custody and supervision order under s. 42(2)(n) capped at 30 days. Unless the Attorney General and the young person agree, no extrajudicial measures or proceedings may start after the time limit in another Act for the offence. Measures and proceedings may continue after the person turns 18, and the Act applies to people 18 or older alleged to have offended as young persons. A youth justice court judge is a justice and a provincial court judge with the powers of a summary conviction court, and a superior court judge deemed a youth justice court judge keeps superior court powers.
ycja.15: A youth justice court has the same power to punish contempt against itself as the provincial superior court of criminal jurisdiction. It has jurisdiction over contempt by a young person against it (in or out of the face of the court) and against any other court out of its face, and concurrent jurisdiction over contempt in the face of another court, and over contempt by an adult in its own face. A young person found guilty of contempt may receive any of the s. 42(2) youth sentence sanctions.
ycja.16: If an offence is alleged to have been committed over a period that includes the person's 18th birthday, the youth justice court has jurisdiction and, on a finding of guilt (after putting the person to their s. 67 election where it applies), imposes a youth sentence if the offence was proven to be before 18 or if it is not proven to be after 18, and any adult sentence if it was proven to be after 18.
ycja.17: A provincial youth justice court may make rules of court, consistent with the Act, other federal law and s. 155 regulations, to regulate the duties of its officers, its practice and procedure, and prescribe forms. The rules must be published or made available to the public.
ycja.18: The Attorney General of Canada or a province, or another designated minister, may establish youth justice committees of citizens to help administer the Act or youth programs and services. Their functions can include advising on extrajudicial measures, supporting victims and facilitating reconciliation, arranging community support and short-term mentoring for the young person, coordinating with child protection agencies, and advising governments on whether the Act's protections for young persons are being complied with.
ycja.19: A youth justice court judge, provincial director, police officer, justice of the peace, prosecutor or youth worker may convene a conference to make a decision required under the Act. A conference can advise on extrajudicial measures, conditions for interim release, sentences and their review, and reintegration plans, or facilitate restorative justice. The Attorney General or another designated minister may make rules for conferences not convened by a judge or justice.
ycja.20: Any proceeding before a justice under the Criminal Code other than a plea, trial or adjudication, and any process a justice can issue, can be carried out or issued for a young person. Despite s. 14(2), a justice may make a s. 810 recognizance order against a young person, but if the young person refuses to enter into it the justice must refer the matter to a youth justice court.
ycja.21: A clerk of the youth justice court may exercise the powers ordinarily exercised by a court clerk, in particular administering oaths or solemn affirmations in court business and, in the absence of a judge, exercising all of a judge's powers relating to adjournment.
ycja.22: The provincial director may authorize any person to exercise the provincial director's powers, duties or functions under the Act, and they are then deemed to have been exercised by the provincial director.
ycja.23: The Attorney General may establish a pre-charge screening program setting out when the Attorney General's consent is needed before a young person is charged. A provincial program already in place before the section came into force is deemed to be one.
ycja.24: No one other than the Attorney General may prosecute a young person without the Attorney General's consent.
ycja.25: A young person has the right to retain and instruct counsel without delay at any stage of proceedings, including before and during consideration of an extrajudicial sanction. An arresting officer must tell an arrested or detained young person of this right and give an opportunity to get counsel. A justice, youth justice court or review board must also tell a young person who is not represented of the right to counsel at a release or detention hearing, a hearing on a s. 14(2) or 20(2) order, a hearing on an adult sentence (s. 71), trial, proceedings on continued custody or conditional supervision (ss. 98(3), 103(1), 104(1), 105(1), 109(1)), a review of a youth sentence and a review of custody level (s. 87). If the young person wants counsel but cannot get it, the court or review board must refer them to legal aid or an assistance program if one exists, and otherwise may, and on request must, direct that the young person be represented, with the Attorney General appointing counsel.
ycja.26: If a young person is arrested and detained, a peace officer must promptly give a parent notice of the arrest, the place of detention and the reason. A parent must also be given written notice of a summons, appearance notice or undertaking, and of a Contraventions Act ticket (other than a parking ticket). If the parents' whereabouts are unknown or no parent is available, notice may go to an adult relative or another suitable adult. If there is doubt about who should get notice, a judge (or a justice if no judge is reasonably available) may give directions. The notice must name the young person, the charge, the time and place of appearance (except for tickets) and state the right to counsel. Written notice may be served personally or by confirmed delivery service.
ycja.27: If a parent does not attend youth justice court proceedings, the court may, if it considers the parent's presence necessary or in the young person's best interests, order the parent in writing to attend at any stage (not in Contraventions Act ticket proceedings). The order is served personally unless the court authorizes confirmed delivery. A parent who fails without reasonable excuse to comply is guilty of contempt, may be dealt with summarily, and is liable to the Criminal Code summary conviction punishment, and the court may issue a warrant to arrest a parent who does not attend after being served.
ycja.28: Except where inconsistent with or excluded by the Act, Part XVI of the Criminal Code (compelling appearance and interim release) applies to the detention and release of young persons.
ycja.29: A judge or justice may impose a condition from s. 515(4) to (4.4) of the Criminal Code in a young person's release order only if it is necessary to ensure attendance in court or for public safety (including victims and witnesses), is reasonable given the offending behaviour, and the young person can reasonably comply. A young person may be detained in custody only if charged with a serious offence, or another offence with a history showing a pattern of outstanding charges or findings of guilt, and the court is satisfied on a balance of probabilities of one of these: a substantial likelihood of not appearing in court; detention is necessary for public safety, including a substantial likelihood of committing a serious offence; or, for a serious offence, exceptional circumstances warrant detention to maintain confidence in the administration of justice (considering the strength of the case, gravity of the offence, circumstances including firearm use, and the likelihood of a lengthy custodial sentence). The court must also be satisfied that no release conditions would adequately address the ground relied on. The Attorney General has the onus.
ycja.30: A young person detained in custody in relation to proceedings must be held in a safe, fair and humane manner in a designated place of temporary detention, and may be held under a peace officer's supervision during transfer to and from court. The young person must be held separate from adults unless a judge or justice is satisfied that, in the young person's best interests, they cannot safely be held in a youth facility or none is available within a reasonable distance. After the young person turns 18, the court may on the provincial director's application authorize temporary detention in an adult provincial facility if in their best interests or the public interest, and a young person who is 20 or older when detention begins is held in an adult provincial facility. The provincial director may transfer a young person between places of temporary detention, and a young person restrained by a peace officer after arrest must be moved to a place of temporary detention at the first reasonable opportunity after appearing before a judge or justice under s. 503 of the Criminal Code.
ycja.31: An arrested young person who would otherwise be detained under s. 515 of the Criminal Code may be placed in the care of a responsible person instead, if the court or justice is satisfied the person is willing and able to take care of and control the young person and the young person is willing. The court or justice must inquire whether a responsible person is available. The placement requires written undertakings from both the responsible person and the young person. The young person can be removed from that care on written application if the person is no longer willing or able, or it is no longer appropriate, in which case the court relieves both of their obligations and issues an arrest warrant, and the arrested young person is taken before a judge or justice without delay.
ycja.32: A young person against whom an information or indictment is laid must first appear before a youth justice court judge or justice, who must have the charge read, tell an unrepresented young person of the right to counsel, and, where notice of intention to seek an adult sentence was given or s. 16 applies, tell them the court might impose an adult sentence on a finding of guilt. Waiver is possible if counsel advises the young person has been informed. If unrepresented, the court must also, before accepting a plea, be satisfied the young person understands the charge, explain adult sentence consequences if applicable, explain the election of mode of trial where it applies, and explain the choice of pleas. If the court is not satisfied the young person understands the charge, it enters a not guilty plea and proceeds to trial (unless an election must be put), and if not satisfied they understand the other matters, it directs that they be represented by counsel.
ycja.33: If a justice who is not a youth justice court judge makes a s. 515 release order for a young person, an application may be made at any time to a youth justice court for release from or detention in custody, and it is heard as an original application. The application needs at least two clear days' written notice (from the young person for release, from the prosecutor for detention), which can be waived. A s. 520 or 521 review of an order by a superior court judge sitting as youth justice court goes to a judge of the court of appeal (in Nunavut, to a judge of the Nunavut Court of Justice), and no such review lies from an order of a justice who is not a youth justice court judge. A young person charged with an offence under s. 522 of the Criminal Code can be released only by a youth justice court judge, whose decision can be reviewed under s. 680 of the Criminal Code.
ycja.34: A youth justice court may at any stage order that a young person be assessed by a qualified person who reports in writing, with the consent of the young person and prosecutor, or on its own motion or application if it believes a medical, psychological or psychiatric report is necessary for a listed purpose and there are reasonable grounds to think the young person has a mental or physical illness or disorder, psychological disorder, emotional disturbance, learning disability or mental disability, has a pattern of repeated findings of guilt, or is alleged to have committed a serious violent offence. The purposes include release or detention decisions, adult sentence hearings, making or reviewing a youth sentence, continuation of custody, setting conditional supervision conditions and authorizing disclosure under s. 127. The court may remand the young person in custody for assessment for up to 30 days, but only if custody is necessary (or desirable on a qualified person's evidence, with the young person's consent), or the young person is already required to be detained.
ycja.35: A youth justice court may at any stage of proceedings refer a young person to a child welfare agency for assessment of whether the young person needs child welfare services, in addition to any other order it can make.
ycja.36: If a young person pleads guilty and the youth justice court is satisfied the facts support the charge, it must find the young person guilty. If the young person pleads not guilty, or pleads guilty but the facts do not support the charge, the court proceeds to trial and finds the young person guilty or not guilty or dismisses the charge.
ycja.37: Appeals for indictable offences (or offences the Attorney General elects to proceed with as indictable) follow Part XXI of the Criminal Code, and appeals for summary conviction offences follow Part XXVII. Where indictable and summary offences are tried or sentenced together, the appeal follows Part XXI. A finding of contempt under s. 15, and its sentence, can be appealed as if it were a conviction and a sentence on indictment. Orders under s. 72(1) or (1.1) and 76(1) can be appealed as part of the sentence and, unless the appeal court orders otherwise, are heard together. If no election is made on a hybrid offence, the Attorney General is deemed to have elected summary conviction. Where the youth justice court is a superior court, appeals go to the court of appeal, and in Nunavut to a judge of the Nunavut Court of Appeal first.
ycja.38: The purpose of youth sentencing is to hold a young person accountable through just sanctions with meaningful consequences that promote rehabilitation and reintegration, contributing to long-term public protection. The sentence must follow the s. 3 principles, must not be greater than the punishment appropriate for an adult in similar circumstances, must be similar to sentences imposed in the region on similar young persons, and must be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence and the young person's degree of responsibility. All reasonable non-custodial sanctions should be considered, with particular attention to the circumstances of Aboriginal young persons. Subject to proportionality, the sentence must be the least restrictive one capable of achieving the purpose, the one most likely to rehabilitate and reintegrate the young person, and one that promotes responsibility and acknowledgement of harm. A condition may be imposed only if it is necessary, the young person can reasonably comply and it is not a substitute for child protection, mental health or other social measures. The sentence may also aim to denounce unlawful conduct and deter the young person. The court must take into account the young person's degree of participation, harm to victims and whether it was intentional or foreseeable, reparation made, time spent in detention, previous findings of guilt, and other aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
ycja.39: A youth justice court cannot commit a young person to custody unless (a) the young person committed a violent offence; (b) the young person was previously found guilty under s. 137 in relation to more than one sentence and, where sentencing for s. 145(2) to (5) of the Criminal Code or s. 137, caused harm or risk of harm to public safety; (c) the young person committed an indictable offence for which an adult would face more than two years and has a history showing a pattern of extrajudicial sanctions or findings of guilt; or (d) in exceptional cases, the aggravating circumstances of an indictable offence make a non-custodial sentence inconsistent with the purpose and principles in s. 38. Where (a) to (c) apply, the court must still consider all reasonable alternatives to custody raised at the sentencing hearing, including submissions on available alternatives, the likelihood of compliance and alternatives used for similar offences. Custody cannot be used as a substitute for child protection, mental health or other social measures, and before imposing custody the court must consider a pre-sentence report (which can be dispensed with on consent) and any sentencing proposal from the young person.
ycja.40: Before sentencing, a youth justice court must consider a pre-sentence report wherever the Act requires it, and may require the provincial director to prepare one if it considers it advisable. The written report includes, to the extent relevant, interviews with the young person, parents, extended family and the victim, recommendations from any s. 41 conference, and information such as the young person's age, maturity, character, behaviour, attitude and willingness to make amends, their plans to change their conduct, the history of previous findings of guilt, extrajudicial sanctions and services rendered and their response, the availability of community services, and the relationship with and control exercised by their parents.
ycja.41: When a youth justice court finds a young person guilty, it may convene a conference under s. 19 to make recommendations on an appropriate youth sentence.
ycja.42: Before imposing a youth sentence, the court must consider conference recommendations, any pre-sentence report, representations by the parties and the young person's parents, and other relevant information. It then imposes one or more of the listed sanctions that are not inconsistent with each other: a reprimand; an absolute or conditional discharge; a fine of up to $1,000; compensation or restitution; personal or community service; an order of prohibition, seizure or forfeiture available under another Act; probation of up to two years; an intensive support and supervision program; a non-residential program (up to 240 hours over six months); a custody and supervision order (custody followed by supervision half as long, totalling up to two years, or three where the offence carries life imprisonment); custody under paragraph (o) for attempted murder, manslaughter or aggravated sexual assault (up to three years); a deferred custody and supervision order (up to six months); a sentence for first degree murder (up to ten years, up to six in custody) or second degree murder (up to seven years, up to four in custody); or an intensive rehabilitative custody and supervision order. For first or second degree murder within the meaning of s. 231 of the Criminal Code the court must impose the paragraph (q) or (r)(ii) or (iii) sanction. A youth sentence other than orders under paragraphs (j), (n), (o), (q) or (r) cannot last more than two years, and combined sentences for different offences cannot continuously exceed three years (with exceptions, including murder). A sentence comes into force when imposed or on a later date the court specifies, and custodial sentences may be ordered to be served consecutively.
ycja.43: If a young person serving an unexpired custodial youth sentence under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) receives an additional sentence under one of those paragraphs, they are deemed to have one youth sentence starting when the first began and ending when the last expires, for purposes of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the Criminal Code, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and this Act, subject to s. 42(15).
ycja.44: When an additional youth sentence under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) is imposed on a young person already serving one, and the combined sentence expires later than the earlier one, the custodial portion from that date is the unexpired custodial portion of the earlier sentence plus an added period: two thirds of the extension where the additional sentence is under paragraph 42(2)(n), the custodial portion extending beyond the earlier one's expiry for a concurrent sentence under paragraph (o), (q) or (r), or the full custodial portion of the additional sentence if it is consecutive. The section is subject to s. 42(15) and s. 46.
ycja.45: If a young person is serving part of a youth sentence in the community or under conditional supervision when an additional sentence is imposed, and s. 44 pushes the end of the custodial portion past the day the additional sentence was imposed, the community or conditional supervision portion becomes inoperative and the young person is committed to custody until the end of the extended custodial portion. If the additional sentence does not change the expiry date, the young person may be remanded to a youth custody facility, and within 48 hours the provincial director must either refer the case to the youth justice court for review under s. 103 or 109 or release the young person to continue supervision in the community or conditional supervision.
ycja.46: If a young person already serving a youth sentence under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) receives a later sentence under one of those paragraphs for an offence committed before the earlier sentence began, the total custodial portions cannot exceed six years, counted from the start of the sentence determined under s. 43.
ycja.47: A young person sentenced under s. 42(2)(n) is deemed committed to continuous custody for the custodial portion. If the sentence does not exceed 90 days, the court may order it served intermittently if consistent with s. 38, but only after getting the provincial director's report confirming a youth custody facility is available to enforce it.
ycja.48: When imposing a youth sentence, the court must state its reasons in the record and give a copy of the sentence and reasons to the young person, their counsel, a parent, the provincial director, the prosecutor, the victim (if the victim wishes) and, for custody under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r), the review board.
ycja.49: When a young person is committed to custody, the youth justice court must issue a warrant of committal. During transfer, the young person may be held under a peace officer's supervision or in a place of temporary detention specified by the provincial director, and the s. 30(3) rule on separation from adults applies.
ycja.50: Part XXIII (sentencing) of the Criminal Code does not apply to proceedings under this Act, subject to s. 74, except for s. 718.2(e) (Aboriginal offenders), ss. 722, 722.1 and 722.2 (victim and community impact statements), s. 730(2), and ss. 748, 748.1 and 749 (pardons, remission, royal prerogative). Section 787 of the Criminal Code (general penalty) does not apply.
ycja.51: When a young person is found guilty of an offence listed in s. 109(1)(a) to (d) of the Criminal Code, the court must, in addition to the youth sentence, prohibit the young person from possessing firearms, cross-bows, prohibited or restricted weapons, prohibited devices, ammunition or explosive substances. The order runs from the day it is made until at least two years after the custodial portion of the sentence ends or, if there is no custody, after the finding of guilt. For an offence under s. 110(1)(a) or (b) of the Criminal Code the court must consider whether a prohibition is desirable for the safety of the young person or others, and if it makes one it runs for no more than two years on the same basis. The court must state reasons in the record, and ss. 113 to 117 of the Criminal Code apply.
ycja.52: A youth justice court may, on application, review a s. 51 prohibition order any time after the period in s. 119(2) (access to records) has ended for the record of that offence. It considers the nature and circumstances of the offence and the safety of the young person and others, and after hearing the young person, a parent, the Attorney General and the provincial director, may confirm, revoke or vary the order, but not make it more onerous. Section 59(3) to (5) apply.
ycja.53: A province may direct that a percentage of any fine imposed under s. 42(2)(d) go to assistance for victims. If it has not, the youth justice court may order a victim fine surcharge of up to 15 per cent of the fine, used for victim assistance as the province directs.
ycja.54: In imposing a fine under s. 42(2)(d), or an order under s. 42(2)(e) or (g), the court must have regard to the young person's present and future means to pay. A young person may discharge a fine or victim fine surcharge in whole or in part by earning credits for work in a program established by the province where it was imposed, or by the province where the young person lives if the provinces have an agreement. The court may consider representations from the person to be compensated and must give that person notice of a compensation, restitution or payment order. An order to compensate in kind or by personal services (s. 42(2)(h)) needs the compensated person's consent. Orders under s. 42(2)(h), (i) or (m) need the young person to be a suitable candidate and must not interfere with normal work or education hours. Personal or community service orders must be completable within 240 hours and 12 months, and community service must be part of a program approved by the provincial director.
ycja.55: An order under s. 42(2)(k) or (l) must include a condition that the young person appear before the youth justice court when required. The court may, in line with s. 38(2)(e.1), also impose conditions such as reporting to and being supervised by the provincial director, notifying of changes of address, employment, education or training, staying within named court jurisdictions, making reasonable efforts to obtain and keep employment, attending school or another suitable program, living with a parent or other suitable adult, living at a place the provincial director specifies, complying with other conditions the court considers appropriate, and not possessing weapons, ammunition, prohibited devices or explosive substances except as the order authorizes.
ycja.56: When a court makes an order under s. 42(2)(k) or (l), it must have the order read to or by the young person, explain its purpose and effect and confirm the young person understands, and give a copy to the young person and any parent present. It may also give a copy to a parent not present who is taking an active interest. The young person endorses an acknowledgement on the order, but failure to do so, or a parent not receiving a copy, does not affect validity. The order takes effect when made and, where the young person also has continuous custody and supervision, runs to the end of the supervision period, and the court can split the order around a delayed start of custody. The young person can be given notice to appear, and if they fail to attend after written notice is proved, the court may issue a warrant.
ycja.57: A youth sentence under s. 42(2)(c) to (i), (k), (l) or (s) may be transferred to a youth justice court in another territorial division, in the same or another province, if the young person or a parent they live with is or becomes a resident there. A judge in the sentencing division may order the transfer on the Attorney General's application, or on the application of the young person or parent with the Attorney General's consent. No transfer to another province can happen until the appeal period has ended or any appeal has been completed.
ycja.58: A youth sentence under s. 42(2)(c) or (k) to (s) in one province may be dealt with in another province under an agreement between them. The court that imposed the sentence keeps exclusive jurisdiction and its warrants and process can be executed anywhere in Canada, unless it waives jurisdiction with the written consent of the Attorney General of the province concerned.
ycja.59: A youth justice court must review a youth sentence other than a custody and supervision order under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r), on application of the young person, a parent, the Attorney General or the provincial director, if there are grounds: a material change in circumstances, the young person being unable or having serious difficulty complying, a breach without reasonable excuse of a s. 42(2)(k) or (l) condition, the terms adversely affecting access to services, education or employment, or any other ground the court considers appropriate. The court may require a progress report from the provincial director and compel the young person to appear. After hearing the young person, a parent, the Attorney General and the provincial director, it may confirm the sentence, terminate it and discharge the young person from further obligation, or vary it or impose a new sentence.
ycja.60: This Part and Part 5 (custody and supervision) apply, with necessary modifications, to orders made on reviews of youth sentences under ss. 59 and 94 to 96.
ycja.64: Before evidence or submissions on sentence, the Attorney General may apply for an order that a young person is liable to an adult sentence if found guilty of an offence committed after turning 14 for which an adult faces imprisonment of more than two years. If the Attorney General intends to seek one, notice must be given to the young person and the court before the plea, or with leave before the trial starts. Notice covers any included offence of which the young person is found guilty for which an adult faces more than two years.
ycja.67: Before a young person enters a plea, the court must put the young person to an election as to mode of trial (judge alone without a preliminary inquiry, judge alone, or judge and jury) if the Attorney General gave notice of intent to seek an adult sentence for an offence committed after age 14, if the young person is charged with first or second degree murder, or if s. 16 applies to a person charged with an offence carrying an election under s. 536 or within a superior court's exclusive jurisdiction under s. 469 of the Criminal Code. The court puts the election to the young person in the wording prescribed in the section.
ycja.69: If the Attorney General gave notice of intent to seek an adult sentence and the young person is found guilty of an included offence for which an adult faces more than two years' imprisonment, committed after age 14, the Attorney General may apply for an adult sentence under s. 64(1).
ycja.71: At the start of the sentencing hearing, the court must hold a hearing on an application for an adult sentence under s. 64(1), unless it has been told the application is not opposed. Both parties and the young person's parents must be given an opportunity to be heard.
ycja.72: The court must order an adult sentence if satisfied that the presumption of diminished moral blameworthiness is rebutted and that a youth sentence under s. 3(1)(b)(ii) and s. 38 would not be long enough to hold the young person accountable. If not satisfied, it orders that a youth sentence be imposed. The Attorney General has the onus, the court must consider the pre-sentence report and give reasons, and the order is part of the sentence for appeal.
ycja.73: When the court orders an adult sentence under s. 72(1), it must impose an adult sentence on a finding of guilt. When it orders under s. 72(1.1) that the young person is not liable to an adult sentence, it must impose a youth sentence.
ycja.74: Parts XXIII (sentencing) and XXIV (dangerous and long-term offenders) of the Criminal Code apply to a young person who has been ordered to receive an adult sentence. The finding of guilt becomes a conviction once the appeal period ends or, if there is an appeal, once all proceedings are complete and an adult sentence is upheld. The section does not change when the adult sentence starts under s. 719(1) of the Criminal Code.
ycja.76: When a young person subject to an adult sentence is sentenced to imprisonment, the court must order that they serve it in a youth custody facility separate from adults, in a provincial adult correctional facility, or, for a sentence of two years or more, in a penitentiary, subject to ss. 79 and 80. A young person under 18 cannot serve any of it in an adult provincial facility or penitentiary. Before ordering, the court must give the young person, a parent, the Attorney General, the provincial director and correctional representatives a chance to be heard, and may require a report. On application (after appeals have expired), the court reviews the placement and, if circumstances have changed materially, may order a different placement. A young person cannot remain in a youth custody facility under this section after turning 20 unless the court orders otherwise.
ycja.77: When a young person is ordered to serve part of an adult sentence in a youth custody facility under s. 76(1)(a), the provincial director must inform the appropriate parole board. Part II of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act applies, subject to s. 78. The appropriate board is the one named in s. 112(1) of that Act where it would otherwise apply, and otherwise the Parole Board of Canada.
ycja.78: Section 6 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act applies to a young person serving part of an adult sentence in a youth custody facility under s. 76(1)(a) only if s. 743.1 of the Criminal Code would send the young person to a prison. Section 127 of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act applies only if s. 743.1 would send the young person to a penitentiary.
ycja.79: If someone serving part of an adult sentence in a youth custody facility under s. 76(1)(a) is sentenced to imprisonment under another federal Act, the rest of that portion is served in an adult provincial facility or penitentiary, as s. 743.1 of the Criminal Code provides.
ycja.80: If someone already serving imprisonment under another federal Act is given an adult sentence of imprisonment under this Act, the sentences are served in an adult provincial facility or penitentiary, as s. 743.1 of the Criminal Code provides.
ycja.81: An application or notice to the court under s. 64 or s. 76 must be made or given orally in the presence of the other party, or in writing with a copy served personally on the other party.
ycja.82: Subject to s. 12 of the Canada Evidence Act, when a young person is found guilty and receives an absolute discharge, or the youth sentence (or a Young Offenders Act disposition) has ceased to have effect, the young person is deemed not to have been found guilty or convicted, other than for a s. 51 prohibition order. Exceptions allow the young person to plead autrefois convict, a court to consider the finding on an adult sentence application, release or sentencing, and parole boards to consider it for conditional release or a record suspension. The discharge or end of sentence also removes any legal disqualification that would follow from the finding of guilt. Application forms for federal employment, Crown corporations, the Canadian Forces and federally regulated work cannot ask about such findings, and a finding of guilt under this Act is not a previous conviction for other offences.
ycja.83: The purpose of the youth custody and supervision system is to protect society by carrying out sentences through the safe, fair and humane custody and supervision of young persons, and to help them rehabilitate and reintegrate as law-abiding citizens through effective programs. The principles include using the least restrictive measures necessary, young persons keeping their rights except those necessarily restricted by the sentence, involving families and the public, and making custody and supervision decisions in a forthright, fair and timely manner.
ycja.84: A young person committed to custody must be held separate from adults, subject to s. 30(3), s. 76(1)(b) and (c) and ss. 89 to 93.
ycja.85: Each province's youth custody and supervision system must have at least two levels of custody distinguished by degree of restraint, and each facility with one or more levels is designated by the lieutenant governor in council (or a delegate for a single least-restrictive level). The provincial director determines the appropriate custody level when a young person is committed under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) and certain other orders, and may later set a different level when the young person's needs and society's interests would be better served. The level should be the least restrictive, having regard to the seriousness of the offence, the young person's needs and circumstances (including proximity to family, school, employment and support services), the safety of other young persons and society's interests, should best match programs to the young person's needs, and must consider the likelihood of escape. The young person and a parent get written notice with reasons.
ycja.86: Provinces must have procedures protecting the young person's due process rights in custody-level decisions under s. 85(3) or (4): the young person gets the relevant information the provincial director has, an opportunity to be heard, and notice of any right to a review under s. 87. The provincial director may withhold only as much information as is strictly necessary to protect safety or facility security.
ycja.87: A young person may apply for a review of a custody-level determination that places them at a level with more than minimal restraint (s. 85(3)) or that transfers them to a higher level or increases restraint (s. 85(4)). Provinces must ensure the review board is independent, the young person gets relevant information (subject to safety and security withholding) and gets an opportunity to be heard.
ycja.88: A province's lieutenant governor in council may order that custody-level determinations and their review be made under the Young Offenders Act instead, in which case the listed provisions of that Act (definitions, s. 11, ss. 24.1 to 24.3 and ss. 28 to 31) apply with necessary modifications.
ycja.89: A young person who is 20 or older when sentenced under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) is committed to an adult provincial correctional facility, despite s. 85. On the provincial director's application, the court may authorize the young person to serve the rest in a penitentiary if that is in the young person's best interests or the public interest and at least two years remain.
ycja.90: When a young person is committed to custody, the provincial director must promptly designate a youth worker to plan the young person's reintegration, including preparing and carrying out a reintegration plan. Where part of the sentence is served in the community under s. 97 or 105, the youth worker supervises and supports the young person, helps them follow the conditions and helps implement the plan.
ycja.91: The provincial director may authorize reintegration leave for a young person in a youth custody facility under s. 76(1)(a) or a s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) sentence: a leave of up to 30 days, with or without escort, for medical, compassionate or humanitarian reasons or to rehabilitate or reintegrate the young person, or release on specified days and hours to attend school or training, obtain or continue employment or do family duties, or take part in a program. A leave can be renewed for further 30-day periods on reassessment, can be revoked at any time, and a young person who breaches it or whose authorization is revoked may be arrested without warrant and returned to custody.
