ycja.92: When a young person is committed to custody under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r), the court may, on the provincial director's application after the young person turns 18 and after hearing the young person, the provincial director and provincial correctional representatives, authorize transfer to an adult provincial correctional facility for the rest of the sentence if that is in the young person's best interests or the public interest. The court may later authorize a further transfer to a penitentiary on the conditions in subsection (2).
ycja.93: A young person in a youth custody facility under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r) who turns 20 is transferred to an adult provincial correctional facility for the rest of the sentence, unless the provincial director orders otherwise. The court may later authorize transfer to a penitentiary on the provincial director's application, if in the young person's best interests or the public interest and at least two years remain.
ycja.94: When a young person is committed to custody for more than one year under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r), the provincial director must bring them before the youth justice court at the end of each year for a review of the sentence (counted from the most recent sentence, or from the earliest where sentences for several offences total more than one year). A young person may also be brought before the court earlier on the provincial director's initiative, or on request of the young person, a parent or the Attorney General, on grounds including sufficient progress or a material change in circumstances: once after the greater of 30 days and one third of the sentence for sentences of a year or less, and any time after six months for longer sentences, or at other times with leave.
ycja.95: Orders under ss. 97(2), 98(3), 103(2)(b), 104(1), 105(1) and 109(2)(b) are treated as youth sentences for the purposes of the s. 94 reviews.
ycja.96: When a young person is held in custody under s. 42(2)(n), (o), (q) or (r), the provincial director may recommend to the youth justice court that the young person be released and placed under conditional supervision, if satisfied that the young person's needs and society's interests would be better served. Written notice with reasons and recommended s. 105 conditions goes to the young person, a parent and the Attorney General, and the court must review the sentence if any of them applies within ten days of service. If no application is made, the court orders release under conditional supervision or, if it considers it advisable, orders that the young person not be released, which may be done without a hearing. The provincial director may then request a review.
ycja.97: Every youth sentence under s. 42(2)(n) must include conditions for the period served in the community: keep the peace and be of good behaviour; report to and be supervised by the provincial director; tell the provincial director immediately on being arrested or questioned by police; report to police or a named person as instructed; give the provincial director their address and report changes in address, occupation, family or financial situation or anything that may affect compliance; and not own, possess or control any weapon, ammunition, prohibited ammunition, prohibited device or explosive substance, except as authorized in writing for a program. The provincial director may set additional conditions that support the young person's needs and reintegration and protect the public, and must read and explain the conditions to the young person and give a copy to them and a parent.
ycja.98: Shortly before the custodial portion of a youth sentence ends, the Attorney General or provincial director may apply for an order that the young person stay in custody for up to the rest of the sentence. The court may order it after hearing both parties and a parent, if there are reasonable grounds to believe the young person is likely to commit a serious violent offence before the sentence expires and the conditions that would be imposed in the community would not be adequate to prevent it. The court considers relevant factors, including a pattern of persistent violent behaviour (number of harmful offences, difficulty controlling violent impulses, weapon use, explicit threats, brutal behaviour, indifference to consequences), psychiatric or psychological evidence of likelihood to commit a serious violent offence, and reliable information that the young person plans one. If the hearing cannot finish in time, the court may keep the young person in custody pending the decision where the application was made in a reasonable time and there are compelling reasons.
ycja.99: For an application under s. 98, the court must require the provincial director to prepare a report on the s. 98(4) factors, in writing unless it cannot reasonably be written (in which case, with leave, orally). Subsections 40(4) to (10) on pre-sentence reports apply. The provincial director must give the young person and a parent at least five clear days' written notice of the hearing, including a statement of the young person's right to counsel.
ycja.100: When a court orders continued custody under s. 98(3), it must state its reasons in the record and give the young person, counsel, a parent, the Attorney General and the provincial director a copy of the order and, on request, a transcript or copy of the reasons.
ycja.101: An order under s. 98(3), or a refusal to make one, is reviewed by the court of appeal on application of the young person, counsel, the Attorney General or the provincial director made within 30 days of the decision. The court of appeal may confirm or reverse the decision, and may extend the time for applying.
ycja.102: If the provincial director has reasonable grounds to believe a young person has breached or is about to breach a s. 97 condition, the provincial director may in writing allow the young person to keep serving in the community on the same or different conditions, or, if the breach is serious and increases the risk to public safety, remand the young person to a youth custody facility until a review. Sections 107 (apprehension) and 108 (review by provincial director) apply to that remand.
ycja.103: When a case is referred to the youth justice court under s. 108, the court hears the young person and, if it is not satisfied on reasonable grounds that a condition was or was about to be breached, orders the young person to keep serving the sentence in the community, on the same or different conditions. If it is satisfied there was a breach or about to be one, it either orders the young person to continue serving the remainder in the community (varying or adding conditions), or, despite s. 42(2)(n), orders the young person to remain in custody for up to the rest of the sentence if satisfied the breach was serious. Subsections 109(4) to (8) apply.
ycja.104: For a sentence under s. 42(2)(o), (q) or (r), the Attorney General may apply, within a reasonable time before the custodial portion ends, for continued custody, and the provincial director must bring the young person before the court. After hearing both parties and a parent, the court may order the young person to stay in custody up to the rest of the sentence if there are reasonable grounds to believe the young person is likely to commit an offence causing the death of or serious harm to another person before the sentence expires. The court considers relevant factors, including a pattern of persistent violent behaviour, psychiatric or psychological evidence, and reliable information that the young person plans such an offence. If the hearing cannot finish in time, the court may keep the young person in custody until the application is decided.
ycja.105: At least one month before the custodial portion of a s. 42(2)(o), (q) or (r) sentence ends, the provincial director must bring the young person before the youth justice court, which sets the conditions of conditional supervision after hearing the young person. The order must include conditions including keeping the peace and being of good behaviour, appearing in court when required, reporting to the provincial director on release, telling the provincial director immediately of arrest or police questioning, reporting to police or a named person as instructed, advising the provincial director of address and changes, not possessing weapons, ammunition, prohibited devices or explosive substances except as authorized, and complying with reasonable instructions to prevent a breach or protect society. The court may add conditions such as travelling directly to the place of residence on release, making reasonable efforts to obtain and keep employment, attending school or a suitable program, and residing with a parent or other suitable adult.
ycja.106: If the provincial director has reasonable grounds to believe a young person has breached or is about to breach a condition of an s. 105(1) order, the provincial director may in writing suspend the conditional supervision and order the young person remanded to a youth custody facility until a review under s. 108 and, if applicable, s. 109.
ycja.107: When conditional supervision is suspended under s. 106, the provincial director may issue a warrant to apprehend the young person, and until apprehended the young person is deemed not to be serving the sentence. The warrant can be executed by any peace officer anywhere in Canada, and a peace officer who believes on reasonable grounds that a warrant is in force may arrest without a warrant. A young person arrested and detained must be brought before the provincial director or a designated person within 24 hours if available (otherwise as soon as possible). That person releases the young person if there are not reasonable grounds to believe they are the person named in the warrant, and otherwise may remand the young person in custody to await the warrant, with release if no warrant is executed within 48 hours.
ycja.108: Without delay after remand to custody following a suspension of conditional supervision, or after being told of the arrest, the provincial director must review the case and, within 48 hours, either cancel the suspension or refer the case to the youth justice court for review under s. 109.
ycja.109: When a suspension of conditional supervision is referred to the youth justice court, the court hears the young person and, if not satisfied on reasonable grounds that a condition was or was about to be breached, cancels the suspension. Otherwise it reviews the provincial director's decision and either cancels the suspension (with power to vary or add conditions), continues the suspension for up to the rest of the sentence and orders the young person to remain in custody, or, for a deferred custody and supervision order, directs that the remainder be served as a custody and supervision order under s. 42(2)(n). The court considers how long the order has applied, any earlier contravention and the nature of the breach, and must give reasons and require a report from the provincial director.
ycja.110: No one may publish the name of a young person, or any other information that would identify the young person as dealt with under this Act. The ban does not apply to a young person who received an adult sentence, or to publication in the course of the administration of justice when the purpose is not to make the information known in the community. After turning 18, a young person not in custody may publish information identifying themselves as having been dealt with under this Act or the Young Offenders Act. A youth justice court judge must, on a peace officer's ex parte application, permit publication of information identifying a young person alleged to have committed an indictable offence if there is reason to believe the young person is a danger to others and publication is necessary to assist in apprehending them. The order ends five days after it is made. A police officer may publish without an order in an urgent situation involving imminent danger to the public, but an order is needed if publication is required for more than 24 hours.
ycja.111: No one may publish the name of a child or young person, or any other identifying information, even if they are deceased, as a victim or witness in connection with an offence committed or alleged to have been committed by a young person. The child or young person may publish it after turning 18, or before that with parental consent, and parents may publish it if the child or young person is deceased. The court may also permit the child or young person to publish if it would not be contrary to their best interests or the public interest.
ycja.112: Once information has been published under s. 110(3) or (6) or s. 111(2) or (3), the publication bans in s. 110(1) or s. 111(1), as the case may be, no longer apply to that information.
ycja.113: The Identification of Criminals Act applies to young persons. A young person charged with an offence can have fingerprints, palmprints, photographs or other measurements taken only in the circumstances in which an adult could under that Act.
ycja.114: A youth justice court, review board or any court dealing with matters arising under the Act may keep a record of any case that comes before it.
ycja.115: Police forces responsible for or participating in an investigation may keep a record of any offence alleged to have been committed by a young person, including fingerprints and photographs, and must keep a record of any extrajudicial measures they use. When a young person is charged with an offence for which an adult could be subjected to identification measures, the police may provide the record to the R.C.M.P., and must do so if the young person is found guilty. The R.C.M.P. keeps those records in a central repository.
ycja.116: A government department or agency may keep records of information obtained for investigating an alleged offence by a young person, for proceedings under the Act, for administering a youth sentence or court order, for considering whether to use extrajudicial measures, or as a result of using them. Other persons or organizations may keep records obtained as a result of extrajudicial measures or for administering or participating in the administration of a youth sentence.
ycja.117: Sections 118 to 129 (the record-keeping and access rules) do not apply to records of an offence for which an adult sentence was imposed, once the appeal period has ended or any appeal has finished with the adult sentence upheld. The record is then dealt with as an adult record, and for the Criminal Records Act the finding of guilt is deemed a conviction.
ycja.118: Except as the Act authorizes or requires, no one may be given access to a record kept under ss. 114 to 116, and no information in it may be given to anyone, if that would identify the young person as dealt with under the Act. People employed in keeping or maintaining the records are not restricted from dealing with one another.
ycja.119: Sets out who may, on request, be given access to court records (s. 114), and may be given access to police and government records (ss. 115 and 116), from the date a record is created until the end of the access period in subsection (2). The list includes the young person, their counsel, the Attorney General, the victim, a parent during proceedings or the youth sentence, an adult assisting the young person under s. 25(7), a peace officer for law enforcement or administrative purposes, a judge, court or review board, the provincial director or adult correctional director, people taking part in conferences or extrajudicial measures, ombudsmen and privacy or information commissioners investigating a complaint, coroners and child advocates, and people acting under the Firearms Act. The access periods include two years after consent to an extrajudicial sanction, two months after the appeal period for an acquittal, dismissal or withdrawal (or a reprimand), one year after an absolute discharge, three years after a conditional discharge, and longer periods for summary conviction and indictable findings of guilt.
ycja.120: Sets out who may, during the period in subsection (3), be given access to R.C.M.P. central repository records (s. 115(3)) for offences listed in the schedule. Those who may include the young person, their counsel, government employees or agents for statistical purposes under the Statistics Act, people with a valid interest whom a youth justice court judge authorizes for research or statistical purposes in the public interest, and the Attorney General or a peace officer investigating an offence where the young person is or has been charged with another scheduled offence or the same one more than once. The name, date of birth and last known address linked to fingerprints may be given for identification purposes. For an indictable offence the access period runs for five years after the period in s. 119(2), and for a serious violent offence where notice of an adult sentence was given it continues indefinitely.
ycja.121: For the purposes of ss. 119 and 120, if no election is made on an offence that can be prosecuted by indictment or by summary conviction, the Attorney General is deemed to have elected to proceed by summary conviction.
ycja.122: A person who is required or authorized to be given access to a record under s. 119, 120, 123 or 124 may be given any information in the record and a copy of any part of it.
ycja.123: After the access period in s. 119(2) has ended, a youth justice court judge may, on application, order that a person be given access to all or part of a record kept under ss. 114 to 116, or a copy, if satisfied that the person has a valid and substantial interest, access is necessary in the interest of the proper administration of justice, and disclosure is not prohibited by another Act; or if access is desirable in the public interest for research or statistical purposes. An application generally needs at least five days' written notice to the young person and the record holder, which the judge may waive if notice would frustrate the application or the young person cannot be found. The order must set out the purposes for which the record may be used.
ycja.124: Despite any other provision of the Act, a young person to whom a record relates, and their counsel, may have access to the record at any time.
ycja.125: A peace officer may disclose to any person information in a court record (s. 114) or police record (s. 115) that it is necessary to disclose in conducting an investigation. The Attorney General may, in a proceeding, disclose record information to a co-accused of the young person, and, to an accused, information identifying a witness as a young person dealt with under the Act. The Attorney General or a peace officer may also disclose information to the federal Minister of Justice for a request to or by a foreign state under the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act or for extradition. A peace officer may disclose to an insurance company to investigate a claim arising from the offence. The provincial director, a youth worker and others providing services to young persons may disclose information to people supervising or caring for the young person, including schools, where necessary, for example to ensure the young person complies with an order.
ycja.126: When records originally kept under ss. 114 to 116 are held by the Librarian and Archivist of Canada or a provincial archivist, that person may disclose information in them if a youth justice court judge is satisfied the disclosure is desirable in the public interest for research or statistical purposes, and the recipient undertakes not to disclose it in any form that could reasonably be expected to identify the young person.
ycja.127: On application by the provincial director, the Attorney General or a peace officer, the youth justice court may order disclosure of specified information about a young person to specified persons if satisfied that disclosure is necessary because the young person has been found guilty of an offence involving serious personal injury, poses a risk of serious harm to persons, and the disclosure is relevant to avoiding that risk. The young person, a parent and the Attorney General must be given an opportunity to be heard, except that the Attorney General may apply ex parte where reasonable efforts to locate the young person have failed.
ycja.128: After the access periods in s. 119 or 120 end, and subject to ss. 123, 124 and 126, no record kept under ss. 114 to 116 may be used for any purpose that would identify the young person as dealt with under this Act or the Young Offenders Act. Records other than R.C.M.P. records may be destroyed or sent to the archivist at the keeper's discretion, while R.C.M.P. records must be destroyed or, if the Librarian and Archivist of Canada requires it, sent to that archivist, at the end of the access period. The section also deals with purging CPIC.
ycja.129: No one who is given access to a record or to whom information is disclosed under the Act may disclose it to anyone else unless the Act authorizes the disclosure.
ycja.130: A youth justice court judge who, before an adjudication, examines a pre-sentence report, or who has heard submissions on sentence after a guilty plea or finding of guilt that is followed by a change of plea, cannot conduct or continue the trial and must transfer the case to another judge. With the consent of the young person and the prosecutor, the judge may continue if satisfied they have not been predisposed by the plea, finding, report or submissions.
ycja.131: A youth justice court judge who takes over from another under s. 669.2(1) of the Criminal Code must, if an adjudication has been made, sentence the young person or make the order authorized by law, and if not, recommence the trial as if no evidence had been taken. If the parties consent, a transcript of evidence already given may be admitted.
ycja.132: A court or justice may exclude any person from all or part of proceedings if the person's presence is unnecessary and the court or justice considers that evidence would be seriously injurious or prejudicial to the young person, or to a child or young person who is a witness or victim, or that excluding any or all members of the public is in the interest of public morals, the maintenance of order or the proper administration of justice. The prosecutor, the young person, their counsel, a parent or supporting adult, the provincial director or agent and the assigned youth worker cannot be excluded. After a finding of guilt, or during a review, the court or review board may exclude anyone other than the young person or counsel, the provincial director or agent, the youth worker and the Attorney General when it is presented with information that might seriously injure or prejudice the young person. These rules are subject to s. 34(9) and s. 650 of the Criminal Code.
ycja.133: Despite s. 478(1) and (3) of the Criminal Code, with the consent of the Attorney General of the province, a young person charged with an offence alleged to have been committed in one province may appear before a youth justice court in another province. If the young person pleads guilty and the court is satisfied the facts support the charge, it finds the young person guilty. If the young person pleads not guilty, or the court is not satisfied the facts support the guilty plea, a young person who was in custody is returned to custody and dealt with according to law.
ycja.134: Applications to forfeit amounts set out in undertakings, release orders or recognizances binding young persons must be made to the youth justice court.
ycja.135: If an undertaking, release order or recognizance binding a young person has been endorsed with a certificate under s. 770(1) of the Criminal Code, a youth justice court judge must, on the Attorney General's request, fix a hearing on forfeiture of the amount and have notice sent by confirmed delivery service at least 10 days before to each principal and surety, requiring them to show cause why it should not be forfeited. The judge may then grant or refuse the application and make any order about the amount.
ycja.136: Makes it an offence to induce or assist a young person to leave unlawfully a place of custody or placement, to unlawfully remove a young person from one, to knowingly harbour or conceal a young person who has unlawfully left one, to wilfully induce or assist a young person to breach a term of a youth sentence or other court order (or a Young Offenders Act disposition), or to wilfully prevent or interfere with a young person performing one. Punishable on indictment (up to 2 years) or on summary conviction. A provincial court judge has absolute jurisdiction to try an adult on the indictable charge, without the accused's consent.
ycja.137: Makes it a summary conviction offence to wilfully fail or refuse to comply with a youth sentence imposed under s. 42(2)(c) to (m) or (s), with a victim fine surcharge ordered under s. 53(2), or with a disposition made under the listed paragraphs of the Young Offenders Act.
ycja.138: Makes it an offence to breach the YCJA's publication and disclosure protections: publishing the identity of a young offender, victim or witness (ss. 110(1), 111(1)), accessing records without authorization (s. 118(1)), improperly disposing of R.C.M.P. records (s. 128(3)) or disclosing information after access (s. 129), along with the matching Young Offenders Act provisions. The Crown may proceed on indictment (up to 2 years) or by summary conviction. A provincial court judge has absolute jurisdiction to try an adult on the indictable charge, without the accused's consent.
ycja.139: Makes it an offence to wilfully fail to comply with s. 30 (designated place of temporary detention) or with an undertaking under s. 31(3) (condition of placement), punishable on indictment (up to 2 years) or on summary conviction. Failing to comply with the matching Young Offenders Act provisions, or using an employment application form in breach of s. 82(3), is a summary conviction offence.
ycja.140: Except where inconsistent with or excluded by the Act, the provisions of the Criminal Code apply, with necessary modifications, to offences alleged to have been committed by young persons.
ycja.141: Section 16 (mental disorder defence) and Part XX.1 (mental disorder) of the Criminal Code apply, with necessary modifications, to proceedings under this Act. Where Part XX.1 requires a copy or notice to be given to an accused or party, it is also to be given to counsel for the young person, a parent who is at the proceedings, and a parent who is not there but is, in the court's or Review Board's opinion, taking an active interest. Failure to give a parent notice does not generally affect validity, but it does invalidate later proceedings unless a parent attends or the judge or Review Board adjourns for notice to be given or dispenses with it. Before making or reviewing a disposition under Part XX.1, the court or Review Board must consider the young person's age and special needs.
ycja.142: Part XXVII (summary conviction offences) of the Criminal Code, and other provisions dealing with summary conviction trial proceedings, apply to proceedings under this Act for peace bond and recognizance orders under ss. 83.3 and 810 to 810.2 (and breach under s. 811), for summary conviction offences, and for indictable offences as if they were summary conviction offences. An indictable offence committed by a young person remains an indictable offence for all purposes. Section 650 of the Criminal Code (accused to be present) applies, s. 786(2) of the Criminal Code (limitation period) does not apply to indictable offences, and s. 809 (costs) does not apply.
ycja.143: Indictable offences and offences punishable on summary conviction may be charged in the same information or indictment and tried jointly under this Act.
ycja.144: A youth justice court judge may issue a subpoena for a person to give evidence, whether or not the person is in the same province as the court. A subpoena directed to a person outside the province must be served personally.
ycja.145: A warrant issued by a youth justice court may be executed anywhere in Canada.
ycja.146: The general law on admissibility of statements applies to young persons, with added protections. A statement by a young person under 18 to a peace officer or other person in authority, on arrest or detention or when there are reasonable grounds to believe the young person committed an offence, is admissible against the young person only if it was voluntary and, before it was made, the person explained in language appropriate to the young person's age and understanding that the young person need not make a statement, that it may be used as evidence, and the right to consult counsel and a parent or other appropriate adult, and that any statement must be made in their presence unless the young person wishes otherwise. The young person must also have been given a reasonable opportunity to consult counsel and a parent (or an adult relative, or another appropriate adult who is not a co-accused or under investigation), and to make the statement in their presence. These requirements do not apply to spontaneous oral statements made before the person could comply. The young person may waive the rights to consult, but the waiver must be recorded on video or audio tape, or be in writing with a signed statement that they were informed of the right being waived.
ycja.147: If a young person is assessed under an order under s. 34(1), no statement made during the assessment to the assessor or anyone acting under their direction is admissible in evidence without the young person's consent in any proceeding with power to compel evidence. Exceptions allow use of the statement for deciding an application for an adult sentence under s. 71, determining whether the young person is unfit to stand trial, making or reviewing a sentence, deciding whether the young person had automatism or a mental disorder exempting them from criminal responsibility (where they put capacity in issue or the prosecutor raises it after verdict), challenging credibility if the young person's testimony is materially inconsistent with an earlier assessment statement, establishing perjury, and decisions on continued custody, conditional supervision conditions, reviews of decisions and disclosure orders.
ycja.148: The testimony of a parent about their child's age is admissible as evidence of age. A birth or baptismal certificate certified by the person holding the record, or an entry or record of an incorporated society that cared for the person around the time they came to Canada (if made before the alleged offence), is evidence of age. Without such documents, or to corroborate them, the court may act on any other information about age.
ycja.149: A party may admit any relevant fact or matter to dispense with proof of it, including one whose admissibility depends on a ruling of law or mixed law and fact. The other party can still call evidence to prove the admitted fact.
ycja.150: Evidence material to the proceedings that would otherwise be inadmissible may be given with the consent of the parties, if the young person is represented by counsel.
ycja.151: Before taking a child's evidence, the judge or justice must instruct the child on the duty to speak the truth and the consequences of not doing so. For a young person, they must give that instruction if they consider it necessary.
ycja.152: Service of any document under the Act may be proved by oral evidence under oath, or by affidavit or statutory declaration, of the person who personally served it or sent it by confirmed delivery service. If proof is by affidavit or declaration, the signature and official character of the person making or taking it need not be proved if the official character appears on its face.
ycja.153: No seal is needed for the validity of any information, indictment, summons, warrant, minute, sentence, conviction, order or other process or document in proceedings under this Act.
ycja.154: Forms prescribed under s. 155, varied to suit the case, or forms to the like effect, are valid and sufficient. Where none is prescribed, forms from Part XXVIII of the Criminal Code, with necessary modifications, or other appropriate forms, may be used.
ycja.155: The Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing forms, establishing uniform rules of court for youth justice courts across Canada, and generally for carrying out the purposes and provisions of the Act.
ycja.156: The Minister of Justice may enter into agreements with a province for payments by Canada toward costs incurred by the province or a municipality in caring for and providing services to young persons dealt with under this Act.
ycja.157: The Attorney General of Canada, or a minister designated by a province, may establish community-based programs that are alternatives to judicial proceedings (such as victim-offender reconciliation, mediation and restitution programs), alternatives to detention before sentencing (such as bail supervision), and alternatives to custody (such as intensive support and supervision programs and programs to carry out attendance orders).
ycja.158: From the date this section came into force, no proceedings may be commenced under the Young Offenders Act for an offence within that Act, or under the Juvenile Delinquents Act for a delinquency within that Act.
ycja.159: Proceedings already commenced under the Young Offenders Act before this section came into force are dealt with as if this Act had not come into force. Proceedings already commenced under the Juvenile Delinquents Act are dealt with under this Act as if the delinquency were an offence occurring after this section came into force. Both are subject to s. 161.
ycja.161: A person covered by s. 159 who is found guilty, other than someone convicted in ordinary court as defined in the Young Offenders Act, is sentenced under this Act, except that s. 42(2)(r) applies only with the young person's consent. A young person being sentenced under this Act while subject to a disposition under s. 20(1)(k) or (k.1) of the Young Offenders Act may, on application of the Attorney General or the young person, have the remaining portion of that disposition treated for all purposes as if it were a sentence under s. 42(2)(n) or (q), unless that would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. For s. 94 reviews, the relevant date is the day the disposition came into force under the Young Offenders Act.
ycja.162: For the purposes of ss. 158 and 159, proceedings are commenced by the laying of an information or indictment.
ycja.163: Sections 114 to 129 (records) apply, with necessary modifications, to records relating to the offence of delinquency under the Juvenile Delinquents Act and to records kept under ss. 40 to 43 of the Young Offenders Act.
ycja.164: Any agreement made under the Young Offenders Act remains in force until it expires, unless it is amended or a new agreement is made under this Act.
ycja.165: Transitional designations: any court established or designated as a youth court under the Young Offenders Act is deemed a youth justice court under this Act, any judge of such a court is deemed a judge of the youth justice court, anyone appointed or designated as a provincial director or youth worker under the Young Offenders Act is deemed appointed or designated under this Act, and review boards and youth justice committees established under that Act carry over. Programs of alternative measures under the Young Offenders Act are deemed programs of extrajudicial sanctions, and places designated as temporary detention, open custody or secure custody carry over to their equivalents under this Act.
ycja.4.1: Extrajudicial measures are presumed adequate to hold a young person accountable for failing to comply with a sentence under s. 137, or for a failure referred to in s. 496 of the Criminal Code, unless there is a history of repeated failures or the failure caused harm or a risk of harm to public safety. In those excepted cases, extrajudicial measures should still be used if adequate; otherwise a judicial referral hearing under s. 496 of the Criminal Code or an application to review the youth sentence under s. 59(1) should be used instead of a charge where that would be adequate.
ycja.6.1: Before starting or continuing judicial proceedings against a young person, a prosecutor must consider whether it is enough to warn the young person, give a caution (if a program exists under s. 8) or, with consent, refer them to a community program or agency, having regard to ss. 4 and 4.1. Failing to consider these options does not invalidate the proceedings.
ycja.24.1: If a charge for which an appearance notice, summons, release order or undertaking was issued is dismissed, withdrawn, stayed or results in acquittal, the Attorney General must review any pending charge under s. 145(2) to (5) of the Criminal Code for failing to comply with that notice, summons, order or undertaking, to decide whether the prosecution should go ahead.
ycja.28.1: A peace officer, youth justice court judge or justice must not detain a young person in custody, or impose a release condition in an undertaking or release order, as a substitute for appropriate child protection, mental health or other social measures.
ycja.30.1: For a young person prosecuted by summary conviction, s. 525 of the Criminal Code (review of detention) is read with '30 days' in place of '90 days'.
ycja.48.1: When imposing a youth sentence, the court must ask the prosecutor whether reasonable steps were taken to find out if the victim wants information about the sentence and its administration, and enter the victim's wishes in the record if known.
ycja.49.1: The youth justice court must give reasons for any credit granted for time the young person spent in detention because of the offence, and state in the record and on the warrant of committal the offence, time spent in detention, the custody and supervision term that would have been imposed before credit, the credit given and the sentence. Failing to do so does not affect the sentence's validity.
ycja.108.1: When a case is referred to the youth justice court under s. 108 and the young person is remanded under s. 102 or 106, ss. 28 to 31 (detention and release) apply to a release application until the court completes its review, with a reference to a young person charged with a serious offence in s. 29 read as a young person who has breached or is about to breach a condition. The young person keeps serving the sentence, subject to s. 107, and existing conditions continue to apply during the suspension. The provincial director must promptly notify the Attorney General.
ycja.109.1: Time a young person spends unlawfully at large while subject to a youth sentence does not count toward any term of a custody and supervision order.
